events.title: Yuanmou Man
events.short: Fossils of Homo erectus found at Yuanmou in Yunnan date to about 1.7 million years ago and are the earliest confirmed human remains in China.
events.detail: Yuanmou Man, also called Yuanmou Homo erectus, is known from two upper central incisors of a single adult, found in 1965 by geologists near Shangnabang village in Yuanmou County, Yunnan. The teeth are robust and shovel-shaped on the tongue side, typical features of Homo erectus. Later, a few crude stone tools, charcoal fragments and animal bones bearing traces of human work were found in the same stratum. Some scholars take this to mean Yuanmou Man may have used fire, though the point remains disputed. Paleomagnetic dating places Yuanmou Man at about 1.7 million years ago, although some scholars argue the date may be as recent as 600,000–700,000 years ago, and discussion continues. Standard Chinese history textbooks use the figure of c. 1.7 million years and list Yuanmou Man as the earliest confirmed human ancestor in China. Yuanmou Man lived in the Early Paleolithic, when the Yuanmou Basin was warm, with forest and grassland and animals such as stegodons and Yunnan horses. He could chip simple stone tools and lived by gathering and hunting. China has one of the largest numbers of early human sites in the world, and Yuanmou, together with Peking Man and Upper Cave Man, provides important evidence for the origin and evolution of humans in East Asia. A Yuanmou Man museum in Yuanmou County displays the fossils and artifacts. The discovery pushed the history of human activity in China back more than a million years.

events.title: Yan–Huang Alliance and the Battle of Zhuolu
events.short: Legend says the Yellow Emperor beat the Yan Emperor at Banquan, allied with him, then defeated Chiyou at Zhuolu; their tribes formed the Huaxia, hence “descendants of Yan and Huang.”
events.detail: Ancient China preserved many myths and legends of remote times, the best known of which concern the Yan Emperor and the Yellow Emperor. Tradition holds that five or six thousand years ago, large tribes such as those of the Yan Emperor, the Yellow Emperor and Chiyou lived in the Yellow River basin, constantly attacking and merging with one another and eventually forming tribal alliances. The Yan Emperor's tribe was active in the Wei River valley in Shaanxi; he is said to have taught people to clear land and farm, made the lei and si plows, planted the five grains, tasted hundreds of herbs and invented medicine, and made pottery and taught people to trade goods. The Yellow Emperor, named Xuanyuan, is said to have built houses, made clothing, dug wells, made boats and carts and invented the bow and arrow; his wife Leizu raised silkworms and reeled silk, and his historian Cang Jie created writing. According to the Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), “Basic Annals of the Five Emperors” and other sources, the Yellow Emperor fought the Yan Emperor at Banquan; the Yan Emperor was defeated and submitted, and the two great tribes formed an alliance. The Yan and Yellow tribes then fought Chiyou, leader of the Jiuli tribes in the east, at Zhuolu (in present-day Hebei) and finally defeated him, and the Yellow Emperor was chosen leader of the tribal alliance. This alliance gradually absorbed neighboring tribes and developed into the later Huaxia people; for this reason the Yan and Yellow Emperors are revered as the common ancestors of the Chinese nation, and Chinese at home and abroad often call themselves “descendants of Yan and Huang.”

events.title: Founding of the Xia Dynasty
events.short: Yu founded the Xia dynasty c. 2070 BC; after Yu's son Qi took the throne, hereditary succession replaced abdication and the world became “one family's,” making Xia China's first dynasty.
events.detail: The Xia was the first hereditary dynasty recorded in Chinese histories. Founded by Yu c. 2070 BC and destroyed by the Shang c. 1600 BC, it lasted about 470 years. During his reign Yu conquered the Sanmiao in the south, built a city at Yangcheng (around present-day Dengfeng, Henan) and set up various institutions. Archaeologists found a walled site at Wangchenggang in Dengfeng, dated to about the 21st century BC, thought to be Yu's legendary capital Yangcheng. In his later years Yu intended to pass leadership to Boyi, but after Yu's death his son Qi took the throne with his strong following, held a great feast for the lords at Juntai and defeated the opposing Youhu clan at Gan. From then on hereditary succession replaced abdication and the “world shared by all” became the “world of one family”; the Three Character Classic puts it as “Xia passed to the son, the world of one family.” The Xia set up an army, made penal laws and established prisons, forming the machinery of a state, and society was divided into nobles, commoners and slaves. Its core area was mainly central and western Henan and southern Shanxi; the Records of the Grand Historian, “Basic Annals of Xia,” records fourteen generations and seventeen rulers, with the surname Si. The founding of the Xia marks the emergence of an early Chinese state, and its hereditary succession was followed by later dynasties. Because no Xia writing has yet been found, Xia history is studied mainly through later texts and archaeological finds such as Erlitou. Later Chinese often called themselves “Huaxia” and “Zhuxia,” and “Xia” became one of the names for China.

events.title: Oracle Bone Script
events.short: Oracle bone script, carved on turtle shells and bones in Shang and Zhou times and found by Wang Yirong in 1899, is China's earliest known systematic writing.
events.detail: Oracle bone script was carved or written on turtle shells and bones of oxen, sheep and other animals in Shang and Zhou times, mainly as records of divination by the late Shang royal house; it is also called “divination inscriptions,” “carved script” and “Yinxu script.” Shang kings divined when matters arose: small holes were bored in the back of a shell or bone and heated with fire, the cracks on the front were read for good or ill fortune, and the date, subject and result were carved on it. The contents concern sacrifices, war, farming, astronomy, illness, hunting and more, a precious source for Shang history. In 1899 Wang Yirong, Imperial Academy chancellor of the Qing, first recognized oracle bone script on “dragon bones” sold as Chinese medicine; afterwards large numbers of bones were found at Yinxu in Anyang, Henan, Zhouyuan in Shaanxi, Shandong and elsewhere. About 150,000 inscribed Shang bones have been found, with more than 4,400 distinct characters, of which about 1,500 have been deciphered. The script already used pictographic, indicative, associative, phonetic-compound and loan methods of forming characters; pictographs make up about 40%, and phonetic compounds had appeared, giving it the basic structure of Chinese characters, and the forms of many characters are still in use. It is the earliest known mature systematic writing of China and East Asia. Scholars such as Luo Zhenyu, Wang Guowei, Guo Moruo and Dong Zuobin contributed greatly to its study, forming the discipline of oracle bone studies. Its discovery confirmed the reliability of the Shang royal lineage in the Records of the Grand Historian and pushed back China's documented history to the Shang. In 2017 oracle bone script was inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.

events.title: Houmuwu Ding and Shang–Zhou Bronzes
events.short: Shang and Zhou bronzes were varied and highly skilled; the Houmuwu ding, 832.84 kg, is the heaviest known ancient Chinese bronze, and the Four-Ram Zun is exquisitely shaped.
events.detail: Copper objects have been found at several sites dating 5,000–4,000 years ago. In the Xia, Shang and Zhou, bronze casting was highly developed, with more objects in great variety, used mainly for food and drink, sacrifice and war. Ritual vessels such as the ding, jue, jia, gui and zun became symbols of nobles' rank and even of state power. Shang nobles loved wine, and the number of bronze wine vessels marked noble rank; the Western Zhou valued ritual, and the numbers of ding and gui marked rank: nine ding and eight gui for the Son of Heaven, seven and six for feudal lords, five and four for senior officials. Craftsmen had by then accurately mastered the ratios of copper, tin and lead and cast fine objects in clay molds, with decorations mostly of taotie, kui dragons and cloud-and-thunder patterns. The Houmuwu ding is a square bronze ding used in late Shang royal sacrifices, found in 1939 at Wuguan village, Anyang, Henan. It stands 133 cm tall, with a mouth 112 cm long and 79.2 cm wide, and weighs 832.84 kg, the heaviest known ancient Chinese bronze; it is named for the three characters “Houmuwu” cast inside (formerly “Simuwu ding”). It is generally thought to have been cast by a Shang king to honor his mother, “Wu.” The Four-Ram Zun, found in Ningxiang, Hunan, has a curled-horn ram at each corner, an imposing form and the largest of the Shang square zun. Western Zhou pieces such as the Li gui, Mao Gong ding and Da Yu ding bear precious inscriptions. Shang and Zhou bronzes represent the peak of world bronze civilization of their time; the Houmuwu ding and Four-Ram Zun are now in the National Museum of China.

events.title: Confucius and Confucianism
events.short: Confucius, founder of Confucianism, taught a philosophy centered on “benevolence,” urged rule by virtue, opened private schools for all, and edited the classics.
events.detail: Confucius (551–479 BC), personal name Qiu and courtesy name Zhongni, was born in Zouyi, Lu (present-day Qufu, Shandong) in the late Spring and Autumn period, of a declined noble family. A keen learner from childhood who studied ritual and music, he served as a minor official managing storehouses and livestock, then opened a private school and became a well-known scholar. In his fifties he briefly held posts in Lu such as magistrate of Zhongdu and Minister of Justice, but soon left and traveled among the states for about 14 years promoting his political ideas, which no state adopted. In old age he returned to Lu to devote himself to education and the editing of ancient texts; tradition says he edited the Poems, Documents, Rites, Changes, Music and Spring and Autumn Annals. His core idea was “benevolence” (ren): “the benevolent love others,” “do not do to others what you would not want done to yourself,” with “ritual” regulating social order. Politically he admired Western Zhou institutions, advocated rule by virtue, opposed harsh government and arbitrary punishment, and urged rulers to spare the people's strength. A great educator, Confucius founded private schools, breaking the nobles' monopoly on education, and held that there should be “teaching without distinctions of class”; he is said to have had three thousand students, seventy-two of them outstanding. He advocated “teaching according to aptitude,” “learning and practicing in due time,” “reviewing the old to know the new,” and the attitude that “to know what you know and know what you do not know is true knowledge.” His words and deeds were compiled by disciples and later disciples as the Analects.

events.title: Iron Farm Tools and Ox Plowing Appear
events.short: Iron farm tools and ox plowing appeared in the late Spring and Autumn period, enabling deeper tilling and land clearing and raising farm productivity.
events.detail: The economy developed greatly in the Spring and Autumn period; especially in its later part, iron farm tools and ox plowing began to appear, a key sign of rising farm productivity. Ancient texts record plowing with iron implements, and archaeologists have unearthed iron farm tools such as hoes, spades and sickles from Spring and Autumn tombs in Changsha (Hunan), Henan, Jiangsu and elsewhere. Most iron tools of the time were wooden tools fitted with an iron cutting edge, much sharper and more durable than wooden or stone tools. By the end of the period at the latest, people were using oxen to pull plows; Confucius's disciples Ran Geng, styled Boniu, and Sima Geng, styled Zi Niu, have names and styles linking “ox” and “plowing,” which reflects that oxen and cultivation were already connected. Iron tools and ox plowing promoted deep, careful tillage and made it possible to clear forests and wasteland and expand farmland; much wasteland became private fields, undermining the land system based on the well-field system. Alongside agriculture, crafts expanded, with growth in bronze, ironmaking, textiles, salt boiling and lacquerware; cast iron appeared in China in the Spring and Autumn period, more than a thousand years earlier than in Europe. As output grew, trade became more active, many cities had markets for exchange and metal currency was used more widely. In the Warring States, iron tools and ox plowing spread further and productivity kept rising; the new landlord class gained strength, laying the economic foundation for the reforms of the states and the formation of feudal society.

events.title: Qin Unifies the Six States
events.short: From 230 BC King Zheng of Qin destroyed Han, Zhao, Wei, Chu, Yan and Qi in turn and in 221 BC founded the Qin dynasty, China's first unified multiethnic state.
events.detail: In the late Warring States, constant war badly damaged the economy and social stability, and people in every state longed for an end to turmoil and for unification. Through Shang Yang's reforms Qin's economy and military far surpassed those of the six eastern states, and it was ready for unification. King Zheng of Qin (259–210 BC) took the throne at thirteen and after taking personal charge removed Lao Ai and Lü Buwei and held all power himself. He recruited talent regardless of birthplace or background, employing Li Si, a minor official of Chu, and Wei Liao, a commoner of Wei; he adopted Li Si's advice to “destroy the lords and achieve imperial rule,” adopting the strategy of allying with distant states and attacking near ones, defeating them one by one, and bribed powerful ministers of other states with gold to sow discord among the six. In 230 BC Qin launched a strong offensive, first destroying Han, then Zhao (228 BC), Wei (225 BC), Chu (223 BC) and Yan (222 BC), and finally Qi in 221 BC, completing unification and founding the Qin dynasty with its capital at Xianyang. During this time Crown Prince Dan of Yan sent Jing Ke to assassinate the King of Qin, without success. After destroying the six states, Qin struck the Xiongnu in the north and conquered the Baiyue in the south, built the Great Wall and dug the Lingqu Canal, and its domain extended east to the sea, west to Longxi, north to the Great Wall and south to the South China Sea. Qin's unification ended the long division and warfare since the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods and created the first unified, multiethnic, centralized feudal state in Chinese history, in line with the trend of history and the wishes of the people, with deep consequences.

events.title: Qin Establishes Centralized Rule
events.short: After unification Qin created the imperial system, with three top ministers at the center and commanderies and counties in the regions, shaping the next two thousand years.
events.detail: After Qin unified China, it created a full system of centralized rule to strengthen control over the country. First came the emperor system: Ying Zheng, regarding his achievements as surpassing the legendary Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, took “Emperor” (Huangdi) as the supreme ruler's title and called himself the “First Emperor,” hoping his descendants would rule for ten thousand generations. The emperor held supreme authority and all military and political power; his orders were called “zhi” and “zhao,” he called himself “zhen,” and he used a jade seal. Second, at the center were set up the chancellor, grand commandant and imperial secretary, the “Three Excellencies,” in charge of administration, military affairs and supervision respectively, checking one another with the final decision resting with the emperor; below them were the Nine Ministers handling specific affairs. In the regions, Qin abolished the Western Zhou enfeoffment system: when Chancellor Wang Wan and others proposed enfeoffing imperial sons, the Commandant of Justice Li Si strongly urged the commandery-county system, which Qin Shi Huang supported. The country was first divided into 36 commanderies, later over 40; each commandery had a governor, a military commandant and a supervising censor, with counties below headed by a magistrate, all appointed and dismissed directly by the court and not hereditary. Below the county were township, village and pavilion units. Qin also made unified laws and applied political, legal, military, land and tax systems throughout the country, so that the emperor and court firmly controlled power everywhere.

events.title: Rebellion of the Seven States
events.short: Emperor Jing cut the lords' lands on Chao Cuo's advice; in 154 BC Wu, Chu and five other states rebelled to “purge the court,” but were crushed in three months.
events.detail: In the early Western Han, Emperor Gaozu Liu Bang, while using commanderies and counties, also enfeoffed a number of kings of his own surname, hoping they would guard the center. As the economy recovered and grew, the kings' power swelled: they held large lands and populations, appointed officials and levied taxes themselves, even minted coins and boiled salt and smelted iron, gradually becoming a regional power threatening the center. Liu Bi, King of Wu, grew rich from minting coins at the copper mountains in his state and boiling seawater for salt and did not come to court for over twenty years. Under Emperor Wen, Jia Yi proposed to “enfeoff many lords and reduce their strength.” After Emperor Jing took the throne he adopted the Plan for Reducing the Domains of Imperial Secretary Chao Cuo and began cutting the kings' lands. In 154 BC Liu Bi, King of Wu, joined the kings of Chu, Zhao, Jiaoxi, Jiaodong, Zichuan and Jinan in a revolt under the slogan “execute Chao Cuo and purge the court,” known as the “Rebellion of the Seven States.” Emperor Jing took Yuan Ang's advice and executed Chao Cuo, but the rebels did not withdraw. He then sent Grand Commandant Zhou Yafu to put down the revolt. Zhou Yafu avoided the rebels' main force, held Changyi and sent light cavalry to cut the Wu–Chu supply line; the rebels, out of food, collapsed, Liu Bi fled to Eastern Yue and was killed, the other kings killed themselves or were executed, and the revolt was put down in about three months. Afterwards Emperor Jing took the opportunity to recover the kings' powers to appoint officials and levy taxes, forbidding the kings to govern their states and leaving them only to live off taxes, reducing the status of the kingdoms to that of commanderies.

events.title: Zhang Qian Opens the Western Regions
events.short: In 138 BC and 119 BC Zhang Qian made two hazardous missions to the Western Regions, opening a route west from the Central Plains, a feat later praised as “boring through the void.”
events.detail: Under the Han, the lands west of Yangguan and Yumen passes (in today's Gansu) were called the Western Regions: in the narrow sense the area of modern Xinjiang, in the broad sense also Central and West Asia and beyond. In the early Western Han the region was divided among many small states, mostly under Xiongnu control, and the Xiongnu used it as a base for raids on the Central Plains. Emperor Wu learned that the Yuezhi had been driven west by the Xiongnu and resented them, so he called for envoys to seek an alliance against the Xiongnu. The court attendant Zhang Qian volunteered. In 138 BC he left Chang'an with over a hundred men. He was held by the Xiongnu for ten years and even married and had a son there, but never gave up his Han envoy's credentials. He eventually escaped and reached the Yuezhi by way of Dayuan and Kangju, only to find them settled in new lands and unwilling to fight the Xiongnu again. On the way back he was detained by the Xiongnu for over a year more, and reached Chang'an in 126 BC with only two of his original party. In 119 BC, after the Han defeated the Xiongnu, Zhang Qian went west a second time, reached the Wusun, and sent deputies to Dayuan, Kangju, the Yuezhi, Parthia, Shendu (India) and other states. Envoys from the Western Regions then visited Chang'an in turn, and contacts grew steadily. Zhang Qian was ennobled as Marquis of Bowang. His missions opened the way to the Western Regions and Central Asia, which Sima Qian called “boring through the void.” They laid the groundwork for the Silk Road, promoted economic and cultural exchange, and prepared the way for the Han to set up the Protector General of the Western Regions.

events.title: Protector General of the Western Regions Set Up
events.short: In 60 BC the Western Han created the Protector General of the Western Regions, seated at Wulei, to oversee the states there, marking the formal incorporation of today's Xinjiang under central rule.
events.detail: After Zhang Qian's mission, the Western Han stepped up its management of the Western Regions. Under Emperor Wu, Han troops campaigned against Dayuan and won its “blood-sweating” horses, and opened military farms at Luntai, Quli and elsewhere under envoy-colonels, securing supplies for envoys and caravans. Under Emperor Xuan the Xiongnu split; the Rizhu king came over to the Han with his followers, and Xiongnu power in the Western Regions collapsed. In 60 BC the Western Han court formally established the Protector General of the Western Regions as the highest military and civil officer for the area. The first holder was Zheng Ji, and the office was based at Wulei (northeast of present-day Luntai, Xinjiang). The Protector General issued Han orders on behalf of the central government, dispatched troops, levied supplies, monitored states such as the Wusun and Kangju, and protected the routes to the west, exercising effective control; at first he oversaw 36 states, later over fifty. His jurisdiction covered today's Xinjiang and the broad areas east and south of Lake Balkhash. Kings and officials of the Western Regions received seals and ribbons from the Han, paid tribute, and sent princes to serve at Chang'an. The creation of the office marked the formal incorporation of the Xinjiang region under central authority, strengthened ties with the Central Plains, promoted the region's economy and kept the Silk Road open. At the end of the Western Han the Xiongnu regained control and contact was briefly cut; in the Eastern Han, Ban Chao spent over thirty years in the region and restored Han authority, and the Eastern Han also established a Protector General and a Chief Clerk of the Western Regions.

events.title: Cai Lun Improves Papermaking
events.short: The Eastern Han eunuch Cai Lun improved papermaking, using bark, hemp waste, rags and old fishing nets, and presented his paper to Emperor He in AD 105; paper gradually replaced bamboo and silk.
events.detail: Before paper, people carved writing on bones and shells, cast it on bronzes, or wrote on bamboo and wooden slips and silk. In the Qin and Han, official documents, letters and books were mostly written on slips and silk; slips were bulky and silk expensive, which greatly limited their use. Later Chinese measure words for books, such as ce, bian and juan, come from the way slips were bound together. In the Western Han people already knew the basics of papermaking, and hemp paper of that period has been found at Fangmatan in Tianshui, Gansu, and at Xuanquanzhi near Dunhuang, but it was coarse and hard to write on. In the Eastern Han the eunuch Cai Lun (d. AD 121), serving as director of the imperial workshops, which made court articles, drew on earlier experience and improved the process, using plant fibers such as bark, hemp waste, rags and old fishing nets, which were chopped, soaked, pounded, formed into sheets and dried, greatly improving paper quality. In AD 105 Cai Lun presented the improved paper to Emperor He, who praised it, and it came into use everywhere as “Marquis Cai's paper.” Cai Lun was later made Marquis of Longting. The raw materials were easy to find, the paper cheap and easy to spread, and its use grew until by the Wei and Jin it had largely replaced bamboo and silk as the main writing material, greatly helping the spread of culture and preservation of texts. Chinese papermaking passed to Korea and Japan, reached the Arab world in the 8th century and then Europe through the Arabs; most papermaking worldwide traces back to China. Papermaking is one of the Four Great Inventions of ancient China and a great contribution to world civilization.

events.title: Zhang Zhongjing and the Treatise on Cold Damage
events.short: The physician Zhang Zhongjing wrote the Treatise on Cold Damage and Miscellaneous Diseases, establishing pattern-based treatment; he is honored as the “Sage of Medicine.”
events.detail: Traditional Chinese medicine has a long history and by the Han had reached a high level. Bian Que of the Warring States summed up the four diagnostic methods still used today; the Yellow Emperor's Inner Canon laid the theoretical foundation of Chinese medicine; and the Divine Husbandman's Classic of Materia Medica is China's earliest surviving pharmacological work. Zhang Zhongjing, personal name Ji, from Nieyang in Nanyang Commandery (around present-day Dengzhou, Henan), was a famous physician of the late Eastern Han. Tradition says that as governor of Changsha he treated patients in his official hall, the origin of the term “sitting in the hall” (zuotang) for a doctor seeing patients. In the late Eastern Han, with frequent wars and epidemics, his clan of over two hundred lost two-thirds in under ten years, seven-tenths of them to cold damage (typhoid-type illness). Grieved, he resolved to study medicine, sought out famous doctors, collected folk prescriptions, and, drawing on earlier work and his own practice, wrote the Treatise on Cold Damage and Miscellaneous Diseases in sixteen volumes. It systematically describes the causes, symptoms, diagnosis and treatment of many externally contracted and internal diseases, proposes the principle of “treatment by pattern differentiation,” matching drugs to a patient's symptoms and constitution, and records many effective formulas, earning it the name “ancestor of formula books.” The original was lost in wartime; edited by Wang Shuhe of the Jin and others, it survives as two classics, the Treatise on Cold Damage and the Essential Prescriptions of the Golden Cabinet. Zhang Zhongjing is honored as the “Sage of Medicine,” also influential in Japan and Korea.

events.title: Western Jin Falls; Eastern Jin Founded
events.short: In AD 316 the Xiongnu state of Former Zhao took Chang'an and the Western Jin fell; in 317 Sima Rui restored the Jin at Jiankang as the Eastern Jin, with “Wang and Sima sharing the realm.”
events.detail: After the War of the Eight Princes, Western Jin strength was badly weakened and the chiefs of the inward-moving peoples rose in turn. The Xiongnu noble Liu Yuan founded the state of Han in AD 304; after his son Liu Cong took the throne, he sent troops in 311 to take Luoyang and capture Emperor Huai of Jin, known as the “Disaster of Yongjia.” In 316 Liu Cong's general Liu Yao took Chang'an and Emperor Min of Jin surrendered, ending the Western Jin. Northern gentry and commoners then moved south in great numbers, the “crossing of the gentry to the south.” At that time Sima Rui, Prince of Langye, a Western Jin royal who held the lower Yangtze, was building his base around Jiankang (present-day Nanjing, Jiangsu); in 317 he took the title King of Jin and in 318 formally became emperor, restoring the Jin with Jiankang as capital, called the Eastern Jin, and Sima Rui was Emperor Yuan of Jin. With no roots in Jiangnan, Sima Rui owed his throne to northern and southern great clans led by Wang Dao, whom he relied on in government, with Wang Dao's cousin Wang Dun in military affairs. People of the time called this “Wang and Sima share the realm.” The Eastern Jin was the age of greatest power for the aristocratic clans; the Wang of Langye and Xie of Chen Commandery held power in turn and imperial power was weak. Northern expeditions by Zu Ti, Huan Wen and others briefly recovered some land south of the Yellow River, but the court distrusted and obstructed the commanders, and the Central Plains were never regained. The Eastern Jin held on in Jiangnan for over a hundred years, successfully resisted the Former Qin at the Battle of Fei River, and kept the south stable, creating favorable conditions for developing Jiangnan. In 420 it was replaced by the Song founded by Liu Yu.

events.date: After the Northern Wei moved its capital to Luoyang
events.title: Carving of the Longmen Grottoes
events.short: Around Emperor Xiaowen's move of the Northern Wei capital to Luoyang, carving began on the Yi River banks; it lasted over four hundred years and left more than 2,300 niches and 100,000 statues.
events.detail: The Longmen Grottoes lie on Longmen Mountain and Xiangshan on both banks of the Yi River south of Luoyang, Henan; the two hills face each other with the Yi water between, like a gateway from afar, anciently called “Yique.” Around Emperor Xiaowen's move of the capital to Luoyang in AD 494, carving began here and continued through the Eastern Wei, Western Wei, Northern Qi, Sui and Tang to the Northern Song, for more than four hundred years, with the greatest number of statues from the Northern Wei and Tang. Longmen now has over 2,300 caves and niches, over 100,000 statues and 2,800 inscriptions. The Northern Wei Guyang Cave, Central Binyang Cave and Lotus Cave are the most representative; their statues have delicate faces and slender bodies with layered drapery, in the “graceful bones and slender forms” and “loose robes and wide belts” style, more sinicized than those at Yungang and reflecting the Chinese character of Buddhist art after Emperor Xiaowen's reforms. The relief Emperor and Empress as Donors, originally in the Central Binyang Cave, showed Emperor Xiaowen and his empress leading attendants in worship and was a masterpiece of ancient Chinese relief carving; sadly it was stolen in the 1930s and taken to the United States, where it is now in museums. The Tang was the high point of Longmen sculpture: the great Vairocana Buddha at Fengxian Temple stands over 17 m high with a full, rounded face and a kindly expression, and is said to have been carved in the likeness of Wu Zetian, who also donated 20,000 strings of cash for cosmetics. The “Twenty Pieces of Longmen” represent Wei stele calligraphy. The Longmen Grottoes, with the Mogao and Yungang caves, are called China's three great grottoes and were inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2000.

events.date: Reigns of Emperors Wen and Yang of Sui
events.title: Creation of the Imperial Examination System
events.short: Emperor Wen of Sui began selecting officials by examinations, and Emperor Yang created the jinshi degree, marking the formal establishment of the imperial examinations, used for over 1,300 years.
events.detail: In the Wei, Jin and Northern and Southern Dynasties the Nine-Rank system was used, and the selection of officials was monopolized by great clans; family background counted for more than ability, producing the situation in which “no commoners among the upper ranks, no gentry among the lower,” and many talented men of humble origin were overlooked. After taking the throne, Emperor Wen of Sui abolished the Nine-Rank system, paid attention to examining candidates' learning, and began selecting officials by examinations by subject. Under Emperor Yang the jinshi degree was created, choosing talent by examination on policy questions, generally taken to mark the formal establishment of the imperial examinations. The Tang improved the system further: Emperor Taizong expanded the state schools and enrolled more candidates; Wu Zetian created the palace examination and the military examination; and under Emperor Xuanzong poetry and rhapsodies became the main content of the jinshi examination. Regular Tang subjects included the mingjing and jinshi, of which the jinshi was the hardest, as in the saying “a mingjing at thirty is old, a jinshi at fifty is young.” The Song added name-sealing and copying of papers, and the Ming and Qing used the “eight-legged essay.” The creation of the examinations was a major change in China's official selection: it ended the great clans' monopoly on careers, widened the sources of officials, let talented men of humble origin join government, and promoted social mobility; and it promoted education and culture. The examinations became the main way successive dynasties chose officials, lasting until the Qing government abolished them in 1905, over 1,300 years in all, and were also imitated by Korea, Vietnam and other countries.

events.title: Emperor Yang of Sui Sends Three Missions to Liuqiu
events.short: Emperor Yang of Sui sent three missions to Liuqiu (today's Taiwan); in AD 610 Chen Leng and others crossed the sea from Yi'an with over 10,000 men, and the Book of Sui has a dedicated account.
events.detail: The Sui called today's Taiwan “Liuqiu.” After the Sui unified the country, seafaring advanced greatly and knowledge of the overseas lands to the southeast deepened. Soon after taking the throne, Emperor Yang sent people to Liuqiu, three times in all. In AD 607 he sent the cavalry commandant Zhu Kuan and the sea master He Man to sail in search of strange customs; they reached Liuqiu but, unable to communicate, brought back one man. In 608 he sent Zhu Kuan again to pacify Liuqiu, but the people did not accept, and Zhu Kuan returned with a local cloth armor. In 610 Emperor Yang sent Chen Leng, a Wuben general, and Zhang Zhenzhou, a grand master of remonstrance, with over 10,000 men from Yi'an (present-day Chaozhou, Guangdong) across the sea to Liuqiu, where they fought the local inhabitants and finally brought back several thousand people. The three Sui missions strengthened ties between the mainland and Taiwan, and the Sui's knowledge of the Taiwan region advanced greatly beyond earlier dynasties. The Book of Sui, compiled in the early Tang, has a dedicated “Account of the Kingdom of Liuqiu” describing in detail its location, products, social organization, food and dress, marriage and funeral customs and religious beliefs. Scholars generally hold that Liuqiu in the Book of Sui mainly refers to today's Taiwan; after Wei Wen's arrival at Yizhou in the Three Kingdoms, this is another important historical record of contact between mainland dynasties and Taiwan. After the Song and Yuan, ties grew closer; the Yuan set up an Inspectorate at Penghu, and Taiwan gradually came under central government rule. These facts show that Taiwan has had close ties with the mainland since ancient times.

events.title: Rule of Zhenguan
events.short: Emperor Taizong of Tang learned from the fall of the Sui, took advice, chose able officials, lightened burdens and perfected institutions. His reign brought clean government and recovery.
events.detail: In 626 Li Shimin, Prince of Qin, took the throne after the Xuanwu Gate Incident, and the next year adopted the era name “Zhenguan”. He is Emperor Taizong of Tang. During his twenty-three-year reign he created an age of good government. Having lived through the collapse of the Sui, he took its fall as a warning, recognized that “water can carry a boat, and water can overturn it”, and valued the support of the people. He was diligent and readily accepted criticism. The minister Wei Zheng spoke frankly, remonstrating more than two hundred times; he put forward the maxim “listen to both sides and you will be enlightened; heed only one side and you will be misled”, urging the emperor to guard against danger in times of peace and to be thrifty. After Wei Zheng died, Taizong said mournfully: “With bronze as a mirror, one can straighten one’s dress and cap; with history as a mirror, one can understand rise and fall; with people as a mirror, one can see one’s gains and losses.” He lamented that he had lost one of his mirrors. Taizong welcomed talent regardless of origin or ethnicity: Fang Xuanling was skilled at planning and Du Ruhui at decision-making, a pair known as “Fang plans, Du decides”. He perfected the system of Three Departments and Six Ministries: the Secretariat drafted edicts, the Chancellery reviewed them and the Department of State Affairs carried them out, each checking the others. He trimmed the bureaucracy and paid attention to selecting local officials. In the economy he applied the equal-field system and the grain, labor and cloth tax system, lightened taxes and corvée, and encouraged agriculture. Abroad, Tang defeated the Eastern Turks and strengthened its rule over the northwest, and neighboring peoples’ leaders honored Taizong as “Heavenly Khan”.

events.title: Tang and Silla Exchanges
events.short: After Silla unified most of the Korean Peninsula it kept close ties with Tang, sent many students, and modeled its institutions on Tang's. Choe Chiwon and others became envoys of Sino-Korean culture.
events.detail: In the Sui and Tang period the Korean Peninsula held three states, Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla, which had frequent contact with China. In the mid-7th century Silla joined Tang to destroy Baekje and Goguryeo, and by about 675 had largely unified the peninsula south of the Taedong River. After it grew strong, Silla was very close to Tang, sending envoys almost every year and many students to the Imperial Academy in Chang'an to study Chinese culture, at most over a hundred at a time. Silla modeled its central and local government on Tang's, selected officials by examinations on the Confucian classics, and adopted Chinese medicine, astronomy, calendrical science, architecture and Buddhism; Tang poetry and books flowed in large numbers to the peninsula. Many Silla merchants came to China, forming communities such as the “Silla quarters” on the Shandong Peninsula and in the Yangtze–Huai region. Silla goods such as bezoar, ginseng, seal skins and gold and silver ware were imported in large amounts, ranking first among Tang imports, while Tang silk, tea, porcelain and books were sent to Silla. Korean music also entered China: “Goryeo music” was performed at the Tang court and popular among the people. Choe Chiwon was an outstanding figure of the exchange. He went to Tang to study at twelve, passed the jinshi examination at eighteen, served as a Tang official, and won fame by drafting for Gao Pian a proclamation against Huang Chao, before returning to Silla. His collected writings, Plowing the Cinnamon Grove with a Writing Brush (Guiyuan Bigeng Ji), survive and are important sources on Tang history and Sino-Korean relations; he is honored as the founder of Korean literature in classical Chinese.

events.title: Tang Calligraphy and Painting
events.short: Tang calligraphy produced many masters, including Yan Zhenqing, Liu Gongquan and Ouyang Xun; in painting Yan Liben and Wu Daozi stood out, and Wu Daozi was honored as the “Sage of Painting”.
events.detail: Tang was strong and culturally flourishing, and calligraphy, painting, music, dance and sculpture all reached brilliant heights. Calligraphy produced many masters. In early Tang, Ouyang Xun's regular script, steep and strict in structure, is called the “Ou style”. Zhang Xu of High Tang and Huaisu of mid-Tang excelled in wild cursive, unrestrained and free. Yan Zhenqing was one of Tang's most influential calligraphers. A loyal official who held Pingyuan and resisted the rebels during the An Lushan Rebellion, he was later strangled while trying to persuade the rebel general Li Xilie, and later generations admired both his character and his writing. His upright, strong and sturdy script is called the “Yan style”, with works such as the Duobao Pagoda Stele and the Stele of Yan Qinli; his Draft Eulogy for My Nephew, written in mourning for a nephew killed in the rebellion, is called the “second-best running script under heaven”. Liu Gongquan of late Tang wrote in angular, bold, powerful strokes, the “Liu style”, and later people used “Yan's sinew, Liu's bone” to describe their calligraphy. Tang painting covered figures, landscapes, birds and flowers and religious subjects. Yan Liben of early Tang excelled in figure painting, capturing both form and spirit, and his Emperor Taizong Receiving the Tibetan Envoy depicts Taizong receiving the Tubo envoy Gar Tongtsen. Wu Daozi of High Tang was Tang's most famous painter, skilled in Buddhist and Daoist figures and landscapes, with vigorous strokes, dynamic lines and fluttering robes, praised as “Wu's sashes flutter in the wind”, and later honored as the “Sage of Painting”. Landscapes by Li Sixun and Wang Wei, ladies by Zhang Xuan and Zhou Fang, and horses by Han Gan were also famous.

events.title: Treaty of Chanyuan
events.short: In 1004 Liao troops marched south to Chanzhou, and Emperor Zhenzong, urged by Kou Zhun, campaigned in person. In 1005 Song and Liao made peace, Song paying annual tribute, bringing a century of peace.
events.detail: After obtaining the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun, Liao came into sharper conflict with Central Plains dynasties. After the founding of Northern Song, Emperor Taizong twice campaigned north to recover the Sixteen Prefectures and failed, and Song then adopted a defensive policy toward Liao. In autumn 1004, Emperor Shengzong of Liao and his mother, Empress Dowager Xiao, led 200,000 troops south, taking cities as far as Chanzhou (present-day Puyang, Henan) on the north bank of the Yellow River, threatening the capital Kaifeng and throwing the Song court into panic. Some ministers urged moving the capital to Jinling or Chengdu, but the chancellor Kou Zhun firmly opposed this and urged Emperor Zhenzong to campaign in person. Zhenzong reluctantly came to Chanzhou and climbed the city tower; Song soldiers, seeing the emperor's yellow dragon banner, cheered and their morale soared. Earlier, Song troops had killed the Liao vanguard commander Xiao Talin with a bed-crossbow outside Chanzhou, dulling the Liao edge, and as the Liao army had pushed far in and feared its retreat being cut, it asked for peace. Zhenzong was also eager to end the war, and after negotiations the two sides made a treaty in early 1005: Song and Liao became brother states; Song paid Liao 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk each year as “annual tribute”; the border was set along the Baigou River, with each side keeping to its frontier and building no new fortifications; and border markets were opened for trade. Because Chanzhou was also called Chanyuan Commandery, it is called the “Treaty of Chanyuan”.

events.title: Bi Sheng Invents Movable-Type Printing
events.short: In the Qingli era the commoner Bi Sheng invented clay movable-type printing, one character per piece, reusable and far more efficient. It is one of China’s Four Great Inventions.
events.detail: China invented woodblock printing in the Sui and Tang. The world's earliest surviving dated woodblock-printed work is the Diamond Sutra, printed in Tang in 868. Book printing flourished under Liao, Song, Western Xia and Jin. But carving blocks was laborious and slow, each block could print only one book, and a single wrong character could ruin a block. After years of exploration, Song printing saw a new breakthrough. According to Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays, during the Qingli era of Emperor Renzong (1041–1048), the commoner Bi Sheng invented movable-type printing. He carved characters one by one in reverse in clay, hardened each by firing to make type. To make a page, he spread a mixture of pine resin, wax and paper ash over an iron plate with an iron frame, set the type inside the frame according to the text, filling a frame to make one forme, then heated it; when the mixture began to melt he pressed the surface flat with a board, and when it cooled the type was fixed on the plate and could be inked and printed. After printing, it was heated again so the mixture melted and the type could be removed for reuse. The method, he noted, “is not simple if you print only two or three copies, but for tens, hundreds or thousands it is extremely fast”. Compared with woodblock printing, movable type was both cheaper and quicker. It later spread to Korea, Japan, Southeast Asia and Europe, some four hundred years before Gutenberg's metal movable type in Germany. Printing is one of China's Four Great Inventions and made a great contribution to the spread and growth of human civilization.

events.title: Shen Kuo and the Dream Pool Essays
events.short: The Northern Song scientist Shen Kuo wrote the Dream Pool Essays late in life, recording movable-type printing, magnetic declination and petroleum, a “milestone in the history of Chinese science”.
events.detail: Shen Kuo (1031–1095), courtesy name Cunzhong, from Qiantang (present-day Hangzhou, Zhejiang), was an outstanding Northern Song scientist and statesman. Learned and versatile, he was deeply accomplished in astronomy, the calendar, mathematics, geography, geology, physics, chemistry, medicine and water management. He took an active part in Wang Anshi's reforms. As head of the Astronomical Bureau he improved observation instruments and revised the calendar, proposing a “twelve-qi calendar” that set months by solar terms, taking the start of spring as New Year's Day with 31-day long months and 30-day short months, which would help schedule farming. In his later years Shen Kuo settled at Dream Brook Garden in Runzhou (present-day Zhenjiang, Jiangsu) and wrote his lifetime's observations and findings into the Dream Pool Essays (Mengxi Bitan). The book has 26 chapters, plus supplementary and continued essays, over 600 entries in all, covering astronomy, geography, mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, medicine, engineering, history, literature and art. It records Bi Sheng's invention of movable-type printing, the most important source for that invention; describes four ways of mounting a magnetic needle and was the first to note that the needle “usually inclines slightly east, not due south”, discovering magnetic declination some four hundred years before Europe; it gave the name “shiyou” (petroleum) to the oil of northern Shaanxi and predicted that “this thing will later be widely used in the world”, a name still used today; and, from conch and clam fossils in the rocks of the Taihang Mountains, it inferred that the area was once seashore.

events.title: Genghis Khan Unites the Mongols
events.short: The Mongol leader Temujin united the tribes of the Mongolian steppe and in 1206 was proclaimed “Genghis Khan” on the Onon River, founding the Mongol Empire and ending long strife on the steppe.
events.detail: The Mongols were an ancient people of northern China, originally in the Ergun River basin, who later migrated west into the Mongolian steppe. Skilled at riding and archery, they followed water and grass and lived as nomads. In the 12th century the tribes of the steppe fought constantly over people, pastures, water and livestock, and people longed for unity and an end to war. The unification of the Mongol tribes was achieved by Temujin. Temujin (c. 1162–1227) came from a noble family of the Mongol Kiyat tribe; when he was nine his father Yesugei was poisoned by Tatars, his followers scattered, and he lived in hardship with his mother and brothers, enduring many trials. As an adult, supported by his father's sworn brother Toghrul, chief of the Kereit, he gradually gathered followers and grew in strength. He was good at employing people, fair in reward and punishment, and knew men's worth. He then defeated the Tatars, Taichiud, Kereit, Naiman, Merkit and other tribes and united the Mongol steppe. In 1206 the Mongol nobles held an assembly at the source of the Onon River, chose Temujin as great khan with the title “Genghis Khan”, and founded the Mongol Empire. After founding the state Genghis Khan organized all herders into units of a thousand, a hundred and ten, a military-civil system of thousand-households, and had the Mongolian language written in Uyghur script, creating the Mongol script. Mongol unification ended the long strife on the steppe and boosted the Mongol economy, and the Mongols entered history as a unified people. Genghis Khan then led armies against Western Xia and Jin and died in 1227 during the campaign against Western Xia.

events.title: Wen Tianxiang Is Executed
events.short: The Southern Song chancellor Wen Tianxiang resisted the Yuan; captured, he refused to yield, wrote Crossing Lingding Ocean and Song of Righteousness, and was executed in Dadu in 1283.
events.detail: Wen Tianxiang (1236–1283), courtesy name Lüshan, art name Wenshan, was from Luling in Jizhou (present-day Ji'an, Jiangxi), and took first place in the palace examination at twenty. In 1275, as Yuan forces came down the Yangtze toward Lin'an, the Southern Song court called on all regions to raise troops to defend the dynasty; Wen responded at once, recruiting over ten thousand volunteers to go to its aid. In 1276 the court appointed him Right Chancellor and Commissioner of Military Affairs and sent him to negotiate at the Yuan camp. He spoke boldly and denounced the Yuan side, and was detained by the Yuan commander Bayan. Soon Lin'an fell and Wen was taken north, but he escaped at Zhenjiang and, after many hardships, reached Fujian, where he continued to organize the remaining Song forces and local volunteers against the Yuan. In 1278 he was defeated and captured at Wupoling in Haifeng, Guangdong. The Yuan general Zhang Hongfan forced him to write urging Zhang Shijie, holding Yamen, to surrender; Wen answered with the poem Crossing Lingding Ocean, whose lines "Who since antiquity has not died? Let my loyal heart shine in the annals" became famous for all time. After the last Song forces were destroyed at Yamen in 1279, Wen was taken to Dadu and held for over three years. The Yuan rulers urged him repeatedly to submit; Kublai Khan received him in person and offered high office such as chancellor, and the captive Emperor Gong of Song was even sent to persuade him, but Wen would rather die, saying, "Beyond death, there is nothing more for me to do." In prison he wrote the stirring Song of Righteousness, expressing his resolve to keep his integrity.

events.date: Reigns of Ming Taizu and Chengzu
events.title: Abolition of the Chancellor and Stronger Imperial Power
events.short: Ming Taizu replaced the Branch Secretariats with three provincial commissions and in 1380 abolished the chancellorship, the six ministries answering directly to the emperor.
events.detail: Zhu Yuanzhang held that the Yuan had fallen because of decentralized local power and over-powerful court officials, so while restoring the economy he took a series of political measures. Locally, he abolished the Branch Secretariats and set up three commissions: the Provincial Administration Commission for civil affairs and finance, the Provincial Surveillance Commission for justice and supervision, and the Regional Military Commission for military affairs. Their heads were appointed by the center, were not subordinate to one another and answered directly to the center, preventing regional separatism. At the center, in 1380 Zhu executed the chancellor Hu Weiyong on a charge of "treason" and used the case to abolish the Secretariat and the chancellorship; the emperor directly managed the six ministries of Personnel, Revenue, Rites, War, Justice and Works, whose ministers answered to him alone, and he held all power himself. The chancellorship, which had lasted in China for over a thousand years, was thus abolished and autocracy was strengthened as never before. As state business was heavy and one emperor could hardly handle it, Taizu appointed Grand Secretaries as advisers. Under Chengzu, Hanlin Academy officials were chosen to serve in the Wenyuan Pavilion and take part in state affairs, called the Grand Secretariat, which gradually became the central body assisting the emperor with government, though its Grand Secretaries could only advise and the final decision rested with the emperor. To tighten control over officials, Taizu also created the secret-police organ the "Embroidered Uniform Guard" answering directly to the emperor, and under Chengzu the Eastern Depot, run by eunuchs, was added.

events.title: Zheng He's Voyages
events.short: From 1405 to 1433 Zheng He led seven voyages to over 30 countries of Asia and Africa, reaching East Africa and the Red Sea, a landmark in the history of navigation.
events.detail: In the early 15th century the Ming economy was prosperous and its power great. The Yongle Emperor sent Zheng He with a fleet to the "Western Seas" (in the early Ming, Southeast Asia west of present-day Brunei and the Indian Ocean region), to "show China's wealth and strength" and develop friendly relations and trade with overseas countries. Zheng He (1371–1433), originally surnamed Ma with the childhood name Sanbao, was a Hui from Yunnan, captured after the Ming conquest of Yunnan and made a eunuch in the palace; he later followed Zhu Di, distinguished himself in the Jingnan Campaign, was granted the surname Zheng and promoted to Grand Director of the Directorate of Palace Attendants, and was known as the "Three-Jewel Eunuch". In 1405 Zheng He set out with over 27,000 men from Liujiagang in Suzhou, putting to sea via Changle in Fujian on the first voyage. Up to 1433 he made seven voyages in all, reaching more than thirty countries and regions of Asia and Africa, as far as the east coast of Africa and the Red Sea. The fleet at its largest had over 200 ships, and according to the History of Ming the biggest treasure ships were 44 zhang long and could hold a thousand people. The ships were loaded with silk, porcelain, tea, lacquerware, gold and silver for gifts and trade, bringing back spices, gems, medicines and rare birds and animals, and Bengal presented a giraffe. The fleet navigated by the compass and by "celestial navigation" using stars, making good use of monsoons and currents. Many countries sent envoys back with the fleet; on the return of the sixth voyage, over 1,200 envoys from sixteen countries and regions came together.

events.title: Qi Jiguang Fights the Japanese Pirates
events.short: Qi Jiguang raised the "Qi Family Army" and devised the "Mandarin duck formation", winning nine battles in nine at Taizhou in 1561 and, with Yu Dayou, largely ending the pirate threat.
events.detail: Ancient China called Japan the land of Wo. In the late Yuan and early Ming, some Japanese warriors, rōnin and unscrupulous merchants formed pirate bands that smuggled and raided along the Chinese coast, known as "wokou". In the mid-Ming, Japan was in its Warring States period while the Ming was weakened and its coastal defenses lax; the wokou colluded with Chinese pirates and shady merchants and raided the southeast coast ever more boldly, killing residents and looting goods, causing great damage in coastal regions, known as the "Japanese pirate troubles". Qi Jiguang (1528–1588), from Dengzhou, Shandong, came from a military family, loved military books from childhood and as a young man set the ambition: "Being made a marquis is not what I want, only that the waves of the sea be calm." In 1555 he was transferred to Zhejiang to fight the pirates. Seeing that the existing troops were slack and weak, he recruited peasants and miners at Yiwu and elsewhere in Zhejiang and trained them strictly; this disciplined, hardy army became known as the "Qi Family Army". To suit the pirates' fighting style and the marshy, water-laced terrain of Jiangnan, Qi devised the "Mandarin duck formation", a 12-man unit combining long and short weapons, balancing offense and defense. In 1561 the pirates invaded Taizhou, Zhejiang in force, and Qi led his army to nine victories in nine battles, ending the pirate trouble in eastern Zhejiang. He then led his army into Fujian and Guangdong and with Yu Dayou, Liu Xian and other generals defeated the pirates, and by about 1565 the trouble on the southeast coast was largely ended. Qi Jiguang was later transferred to Jizhen as garrison commander, guarding the northern frontier for sixteen years and overseeing the building of the Great Wall.

events.title: The Travel Diaries of Xu Xiake
events.short: Over thirty years Xu Xiake traveled much of China; his diaries became The Travel Diaries of Xu Xiake, with limestone-landform studies among the world's most advanced of the time.
events.detail: Xu Xiake (1587–1641), given name Hongzu, art name Xiake, was from Jiangyin in Nanzhili (present-day Jiangyin, Jiangsu). From childhood he loved books on geography, history and travel and exploration, set the ambition that "a real man should be at the blue sea in the morning and Cangwu in the evening", and was unwilling to take the examination path to office. With his mother's support he began traveling at 22, and over more than thirty years his footprints covered a dozen present-day provinces and regions, much of China. He traveled mainly on foot, often climbing cliffs and entering caves in the face of great danger. In 1636 Xu began his last and longest "ten-thousand-li journey", going through Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Hunan, Guangxi and Guizhou to Yunnan, as far as Tengchong in western Yunnan; in 1640 he was brought home ill and died the next year. He insisted on writing a diary every day recording his observations, leaving over 600,000 characters of travel material, later compiled as The Travel Diaries of Xu Xiake. The book records in detail natural phenomena such as geography, hydrology, geology and plants in each place, along with economy, transport, towns and villages and local customs. He systematically surveyed and described the limestone (karst) landforms of Guangxi, Guizhou and Yunnan and analyzed the origin of caves and peaks, ahead of comparable European studies; he also established that the Jinsha River is the upper course of the Yangtze, correcting the old view that "the Min Mountains are the source of the Yangtze". Xu's descriptions are concrete and vivid, blending scene and feeling, and the Diaries are both a great geographic work and a literary classic.

events.title: The Chengde Mountain Resort
events.short: The Qing built the Chengde Mountain Resort and the Eight Outer Temples, where emperors handled state affairs and received envoys and ethnic leaders, reflecting its policy of ethnic unity.
events.detail: The Chengde Mountain Resort, in present-day Chengde, Hebei, also called the Rehe Travel Palace, was where Qing emperors spent the summer and handled state affairs. The Kangxi Emperor set up the Mulan hunting ground north of Chengde, where each autumn he led princes, ministers and Eight Banners troops to hunt and practice martial skills, called the "Mulan autumn hunt". In 1703 he ordered a travel palace built at Chengde; over the Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong reigns, nearly ninety years, it was completed in 1792. The Resort covers about 5.64 million square meters and is the largest surviving classical imperial garden in China, divided into a palace area and a garden area with lakes, plains and mountains, recalling both the water towns of Jiangnan and the grasslands north of the Wall; Kangxi and Qianlong named "seventy-two scenes". Each year the Qing designated Mongol princes in turn to come to the Resort to accompany the emperor in hunting and martial exercises and gave them rewards; Uyghur, Tibetan and other minority leaders also often came to pay their respects. In 1771 the Qianlong Emperor received here Ubashi, leader of the Torghut Mongols who had returned from the Volga; in 1780 the Sixth Panchen Lama came to congratulate him on his birthday; and in 1793 he received the British Macartney mission here. To unite the Mongols, Tibetans and other minorities, the Qing built twelve grand temples outside the Resort, popularly the "Eight Outer Temples", blending Han, Tibetan and Mongol architectural styles; the Putuo Zongcheng Temple was modeled on the Potala Palace in Lhasa and the Temple of Sumeru Happiness and Longevity on Tashilhunpo Monastery in Shigatse. In 1994 the Resort and the surrounding temples were inscribed on the World Heritage List.

events.title: Population Reaches 300 Million
events.short: In the early Qing, social stability and economic growth made the population surge; by the end of the Qianlong reign it reached 300 million, about a third of the world’s total.
events.detail: At the height of the Ming dynasty China’s population exceeded 100 million. Economic decline and years of war from the late Ming sharply reduced it. In the early Qing, the rulers took measures to restore the economy; society was stable, and the population rose greatly. By the Kangxi reign it had reached about 150 million. By the end of the Qianlong reign it was 300 million, roughly a third of the world’s population, and in the Daoguang era it passed 400 million. There were many causes. Long-term stability and economic growth provided the conditions; high-yield crops such as maize, sweet potatoes and potatoes spread, greatly raising grain output and feeding more people; and after the policies of “increasing population without ever raising taxes” and “merging the poll tax into the land tax,” the poll tax was no longer levied per head, people no longer had to hide their numbers, and official figures came closer to reality. The growth supplied ample labor and promoted the development of frontier and mountain areas, as many inland farmers moved to the Northeast, Inner Mongolia, Taiwan and the southwestern mountains. But population grew far faster than farmland, so land per person kept shrinking and the problem of “many people, little land” became acute; with serious land concentration, many peasants lost their land and became drifters, and social tensions mounted. The late Qianlong scholar Hong Liangji pointed out in his essay Zhiping Pian that population was growing far faster than fields and houses, which would bring serious social problems. The population problem became one root of the Qing’s mid-to-late social crisis.

events.title: The Opium War and the Treaty of Nanjing
events.short: Britain launched the Opium War in 1840; the Qing was defeated and in 1842 forced to sign the Treaty of Nanjing, the first unequal treaty of modern times, marking the start of modern Chinese history.
events.detail: When news of Lin Zexu’s destruction of opium reached London, the British government decided to wage war on China. In June 1840 a British expeditionary force reached the Guangdong coast and the Opium War began. Finding Guangdong well defended, the British moved north, took Dinghai in Zhejiang and reached the mouth of the Baihe River near Tianjin, threatening the Qing court. The panicking Daoguang Emperor dismissed Lin Zexu for “mismanagement” and sent Qishan to negotiate in Guangdong. During the talks, in January 1841 the British seized the Shajiao and Dajiao forts at Humen and occupied Hong Kong Island. The emperor was forced to declare war; in February the British took the Humen forts, and naval commander Guan Tianpei fought to the death. The war then widened: Dinghai fell again, with three brigade generals including Ge Yunfei killed; Zhenhai fell, and Governor-General Yuqian drowned himself. In 1842 the British entered the Yangtze, took the Wusong forts, where Chen Huacheng was killed, and then Zhenjiang. In August British warships reached Nanjing, and the Qing sued for peace and signed the Treaty of Nanjing. It ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain; required an indemnity of 21 million silver dollars; opened Guangzhou, Xiamen, Fuzhou, Ningbo and Shanghai as treaty ports; and required China to agree tariffs on British goods with Britain. The first unequal treaty in modern Chinese history, it gravely damaged China’s territorial sovereignty and tariff autonomy and began China’s slide into a semi-colonial, semi-feudal society. The Opium War marks the start of modern Chinese history, when the Chinese people began their struggle against foreign aggression and for national independence.

events.title: Taiping Capital at Tianjing and the Land System
events.short: In 1853 the Taiping army took Nanjing, renamed it Tianjing and made it the capital, issuing the Land System of the Heavenly Dynasty with its ideal of “farming land together, eating together,” which could not be put into practice.
events.detail: In spring 1852 the Taiping army broke out of Yong’an and marched north, besieging Guilin and Changsha. South King Feng Yunshan and West King Xiao Chaogui both died on the march. In January 1853 it took Wuchang, capital of Hubei, and grew to 500,000 men. It then left Wuchang and advanced east along the Yangtze by land and water, taking Jiujiang, Anqing, Wuhu and other places, and in March 1853 captured Nanjing, renamed it Tianjing (Heavenly Capital) and made it the capital, formally establishing a peasant regime facing the Qing. There it issued the Land System of the Heavenly Dynasty, which divided land into nine grades by yield and distributed it equally by population and age regardless of sex, with those over sixteen receiving a full share and those fifteen and under half. Every twenty-five families formed a unit with a public treasury and a worship hall, and each household kept only the grain it needed and handed the rest to the treasury. It set out an ideal society in which “land is farmed together, food is eaten together, clothes are worn together, money is spent together, everything is evenly shared, and no one lacks food or warmth.” The system reflected the peasants’ strong wish to abolish feudal land ownership and gain land, and served as a programmatic document of anti-feudal struggle, but its strong absolute egalitarianism was divorced from reality and could not be carried out. In practice the Taiping in its territory kept the policy of “paying grain and taxes as before.” It also sent northern and western expeditions: the northern force pushed deep alone, came close to Tianjin and ultimately failed, while the western force won great victories and took much of the middle Yangtze.

events.title: Founding of Shen Bao
events.short: In 1872 the British merchant Ernest Major founded Shen Bao in Shanghai; later run by Chinese owners until it closed in 1949, it was among modern China’s longest-running and most influential Chinese newspapers.
events.detail: After the Opium War, foreigners founded many newspapers and periodicals in Hong Kong, Shanghai and elsewhere, at first mainly for foreign readers in China, though Chinese-language papers soon appeared. On 30 April 1872 the British merchant Ernest Major and partners founded Shen Bao in Shanghai, originally called Shenjiang Xinbao (“Shen” is another name for Shanghai). It hired Chinese literati as chief writers and carried news, commentary, market prices, advertisements and literary works, suiting Chinese readers’ habits at a low price, and quickly found a market. It sent reporters out early and reported social news such as the “Yang Naiwu and Xiao Baicai” case at length, drawing wide attention. In 1882 it first used the telegraph to transmit news, greatly improving timeliness. In 1909 it was bought by the Chinese comprador Xi Zipei, and in 1912 Shi Liangcai and others took it over, after which it grew into one of the country’s most influential papers. In the 1930s its supplement Free Talk published many articles by writers such as Lu Xun and Mao Dun. After the Mukden Incident it actively promoted resistance to Japan and criticized the Nationalist government’s policy of “internal pacification before external resistance.” In 1934 Shi Liangcai was assassinated by Nationalist agents. After Shanghai’s liberation in May 1949 Shen Bao ceased publication, having published over 25,000 issues. It recorded 77 years of modern Chinese history and has been called an “encyclopedia” for studying modern China. The appearance of modern newspapers accelerated the spread of information and helped change social attitudes and advance ideas.

events.title: Zhang Jian Founds Dasheng Cotton Mill and “Saving the Nation through Industry”
events.short: After the war, top scholar Zhang Jian gave up an official career to found the Dasheng Cotton Mill in his native Nantong, later a conglomerate, and founded schools, a leading figure of “saving the nation through industry.”
events.detail: In the 1860s and 1870s Chinese national capitalism appeared but grew slowly. After the Sino-Japanese War foreign capital opened factories and mines in China, and some patriots put forward “saving the nation through industry,” giving national industry an initial boost. Zhang Jian (1853–1926), courtesy name Jizhi, from Nantong, Jiangsu, became the top scholar (zhuangyuan) in the 1894 examinations and was appointed a Hanlin compiler. The defeat and the Treaty of Shimonoseki shocked him; holding that “industry and education support each other,” he resolutely gave up an official career and returned home to start enterprises. In 1895, at the request of Zhang Zhidong, Governor-General of Liangjiang, he began planning a cotton mill in Nantong, and the Dasheng Cotton Mill opened in 1899; “Dasheng” comes from the Book of Changes line “the great virtue of heaven and earth is to give life.” Using Nantong’s cotton, the mill produced good yarn with wide sales. Zhang then founded a land reclamation company, oil mill, flour mill, steamship company and more, forming the Dasheng group, one of the largest national capitalist groups of the time. He also supported education and public welfare, founding Tongzhou Normal School (China’s first independent normal school), the Nantong Museum (the first museum founded by Chinese), a library, a hospital and a home for the aged, making Nantong a nationally known model city. After the 1911 Revolution he served as Minister of Agriculture and Commerce of the Beiyang government. His work led many Chinese to “save the nation through industry” and boosted national capitalism; Mao Zedong said that in discussing light industry one must not forget Zhang Jian.

events.title: The Tongmenghui and the Three Principles of the People
events.short: In 1905 Sun Yat-sen united the Revive China Society, China Revival Society, Restoration Society and others in Tokyo to found the Tongmenghui, proposing the Three Principles of the People, the first national bourgeois revolutionary party.
events.detail: In the early 20th century revolutionary groups sprang up in many places, but they were scattered and fought separately, and the revolution urgently needed a unified organization. On 20 August 1905 Sun Yat-sen united the Revive China Society, China Revival Society, Restoration Society and others and founded the Tongmenghui (Chinese Revolutionary Alliance) in Tokyo, Japan. Sun was elected premier, Huang Xing became head of the executive department, and branches were set up at home and abroad. Its political program was to “expel the Tartars, restore China, establish a republic and equalize land rights,” and it founded the Min Bao. In November Sun’s foreword to the Min Bao summarized the program as three principles, nationalism, democracy and people’s livelihood, the “Three Principles of the People.” Nationalism meant “expelling the Tartars and restoring China,” overthrowing Qing rule by revolution; democracy meant “establishing a republic,” overthrowing feudal monarchy and founding a bourgeois democratic republic; people’s livelihood meant “equalizing land rights,” fixing land prices. The Three Principles were a fairly complete bourgeois democratic program and became the guiding ideology of the 1911 Revolution, though they did not clearly oppose imperialism or propose a thorough anti-feudal land program. After its founding the Tongmenghui used the Min Bao to wage a great debate with royalists led by Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao over whether to overthrow the Qing by revolution, and launched many armed uprisings. It was China’s first national bourgeois revolutionary party, and its founding marked a new stage of the bourgeois democratic revolution.

events.title: Wuchang Uprising and the Xinhai Revolution
events.short: On 10 October 1911 revolutionaries in the Hubei New Army launched the Wuchang Uprising; provinces declared independence one after another and Qing rule swiftly collapsed.
events.detail: In May 1911 the Qing government formed a “Royal Cabinet” dominated by imperial clansmen and announced the “nationalization of railways”, taking over the Sichuan–Hankou and Guangzhou–Hankou lines that had been built with private funds. This provoked railway protection movements in Hunan, Hubei, Guangdong and Sichuan; in Sichuan the movement was fiercest and grew into an armed uprising. Meanwhile, the Hubei revolutionary groups Literary Society and Progressive Association, encouraged by the Tongmenghui, had recruited many members in the New Army and were planning an uprising. On 9 October, Sun Wu, a leader of the Progressive Association, accidentally set off a bomb while making explosives in the Russian concession at Hankou; the plan was exposed and the government made mass arrests from its lists of revolutionaries. In this desperate situation, on the night of 10 October, revolutionaries of the New Army's Eighth Engineer Battalion, led by Xiong Bingkun, were the first to act and fired the first shot of the Wuchang Uprising. After a night of fighting the rebels held Wuchang, and Hanyang and Hankou were soon recovered. They established the Hubei Military Government and chose Li Yuanhong, a New Army brigade commander, as military governor. Hunan, Shaanxi and other provinces followed, and within a little over a month more than ten provinces declared independence from the Qing, whose rule swiftly collapsed. Because 1911 was the xinhai year of the traditional calendar, the revolution is called the Xinhai Revolution. It overthrew the monarchy that had ruled China for over two thousand years, established the Republic of China and planted the idea of democratic republicanism in people's minds; it was a great bourgeois democratic revolution in modern Chinese history.

events.title: Founding of the Republic of China
events.short: On 1 January 1912 Sun Yat-sen took office in Nanjing as provisional president, proclaiming the Republic of China, the first bourgeois republic in Chinese history.
events.detail: After the Wuchang Uprising succeeded, provinces declared independence one after another, and the revolution needed a unified central government. In December 1911 Sun Yat-sen returned to Shanghai from abroad. On 29 December, delegates of seventeen provinces met in Nanjing and elected Sun provisional president. On 1 January 1912 Sun was sworn in at Nanjing, proclaiming the founding of the Republic of China, with Nanjing as its capital, the Gregorian calendar adopted, and 1912 as Year 1 of the Republic. In his inaugural declaration he stated that the lands of the Han, Manchu, Mongol, Hui and Tibetan peoples were united as one country, and those peoples as one: the “Five Races Under One Union”. The Nanjing Provisional Government headed by Sun was then formed, with a Provisional Senate as its legislature. It issued a series of decrees to sweep away the old and bring in the new. Politically, it guaranteed democratic rights, abolished titles such as “Your Excellency” and “Master”, and banned the trade in people. Economically, it encouraged industry and protected private property. In social customs, it ordered queues cut and banned foot-binding, gambling and opium smoking. In education, it abolished the study of the classics and promoted modern schooling. These measures favored capitalist development and changed social attitudes. The founding of the Republic established the first bourgeois republic in Chinese history and planted the idea of democratic republicanism in people's minds. But the Nanjing Provisional Government lasted only briefly: facing pressure from imperialist powers and financial difficulties, Sun was forced to compromise with Yuan Shikai, and just three months later the provisional government moved to Beijing.

events.title: Song Jiaoren's Assassination and Second Revolution
events.short: In 1913 the Kuomintang won the elections and Song Jiaoren was assassinated in Shanghai; Sun Yat-sen's “Second Revolution” against Yuan Shikai failed within two months.
events.detail: After becoming provisional president, Yuan Shikai repeatedly undermined the responsible cabinet system. Song Jiaoren, a Tongmenghui member, hoped to limit Yuan's power through parliamentary elections and a party cabinet. In August 1912 he built on the Tongmenghui and merged several other parties to form the Kuomintang. In the first parliamentary elections, from late 1912 to early 1913, the Kuomintang won a majority of seats in both houses and became the largest party, and Song prepared to form a responsible cabinet as leader of the majority party. On 20 March 1913, as Song was about to board a train north at Shanghai railway station, he was shot by an assassin and died, aged only 30. Investigation showed that the masterminds were linked to Yuan Shikai's government. Sun Yat-sen saw Yuan's reactionary face and called for armed action against him. In April, without parliamentary approval, Yuan took a loan of 25 million pounds from a five-nation banking consortium of Britain, France, Germany, Russia and Japan, the “Reorganization Loan”. He then dismissed Li Liejun, military governor of Jiangxi, Hu Hanmin of Guangdong and Bai Wenwei of Anhui. In July Li Liejun declared independence at Hukou in Jiangxi and raised troops against Yuan; Huang Xing responded in Nanjing, and Anhui, Guangdong, Hunan and other provinces followed. This is known as the “Second Revolution”. But because of divisions and lack of cohesion within the Kuomintang, Yuan crushed it in under two months, and Sun, Huang Xing and others were forced into exile in Japan. Its failure showed that a bourgeois republic would not work in China. In 1914 Sun formed the Chinese Revolutionary Party in Japan to continue the struggle against Yuan.
